verifyText.value: Negotiating the best possible deal on a new car purchase takes preparation.
Create a List of What's Most Important to You

Decide on the vehicle type, the gas mileage you want, V-8 or V-6, storage space necessities, luxury items or not, navigational system, etc. and identify features that you can and can't live without. This will help you narrow your options down to the vehicle that best meets your needs. Then search the Internet for the make, model and year and start price comparison shopping to arrive at the going rate for the car you want.
Determine The Price You Can Afford and Qualify For

Now that you have narrowed down the type of car you want, take a look at your budget to ensure you can afford this car over time. Knowing where you stand before entering the negotiations process with the dealership gives you the strongest position. Do not compromise on the amount you are willing to pay. Be aware of your credit score and get preapproved financing so you have the current rates and know your bottom line. If they want to make a deal, they will have to beat the offer in hand. Remember, even after the salesman gives you the price, the finance manager's going to entice you to add many features that will increase the overall cost of the vehicle along with your monthly payments.

A fair offer to both sides is one that is 3% - 5% over the actual dealer's cost, not above the invoice price. The true dealer cost (what they paid to the manufacturer) is decidedly less than the invoice price. This results from to a variety of discounts offered to the dealer, such as dealer holdback and factory-to-dealer dealer incentives, that do not appear on the invoice. Exactly how much a dealer pays a carmaker for a vehicle is an elusive figure. Sites like TrueCar and Edmunds can help you eliminate the guesswork and determine a fair selling price for a vehicle.
Make Dealers Compete for Your Business

After obtaining an estimate of the dealer's actual cost and determining a fair price, pit against each other to get you the best deal. Solicit bids from several dealers, via e-mail, over the phone, or in person.
Be Calm, Methodical, and Walk Away if Necessary

Don't become emotional and remain friendly and courteous. Always settle negotiations on the sales price before discussing monthly payment, trade-in value or financing options. But move one step at a time so you do not lose focus of the big picture and let things get ahead of you. . If you're finding the seller is aggressive and overpowering don't fear be prepared to walk away. They will be more inclined to make a deal when you make them sweat.

If an automaker offers you low rate financing, taking it often means having to pass on a rebate, since typically you will not receive both. But you often can get the best of both worlds by taking the rebate from the dealer and getting financing elsewhere, even if the interest rate is higher than the promotional one from the manufacturer. Visit LotPro for a list of all the national new car incentives published by the auto makers. Understanding the incentives being offered and when they expire can give you an upper hand in the negotiations.

Tips for Buying a Used Car

waitForText.value: Tips for Buying a Used Car

verifyText.value: Always Get a CARFAX History Report

A CARFAX report is a quick and inexpensive way to get the history of the car informing you of any major accidents, odometer reading discrepancy, number of owners and other pertinent information that could impact your vehicle purchase. This will let you know things the owner may not know or choose to disclose.
Private Party is Usually Less Expensive than Dealer

A dealer is going to try to mark up the car and the financing, adding in as many additional costs as possible to make you pay the most for the car. The individual car seller is simply trying to sell the car. It's usually a simple one-time payment and exchange of ownership information followed by a trip to the DMV. Note that although the dealer will generally cost you more money, you may be eligible for guarantees the private seller cannot give you like an extended warranty. If you found the perfect car at the right place, shop around for the additional features.
Dealerships Must Stand By the Car

There is something to be said for the security of legal protection. Dealerships all carry the warranty of merchantability, and cannot knowingly sell a car below standards. The law provides substantial protection to a consumer from basic operating problems at the time of purchase. If you bought a car that is not up to standards even without an extended warranty, you are entitled to legal recourse.
Private Sellers Do Not Have Guarantees

There is no warranty of merchantability requirement for John Doe selling his car on Craigslist. Your due diligence must now come into play. Go the extra step to have the car taken in for examination by a certified mechanic specifically for that make/model vehicle. Ask for a history of repairs, oil changes and other services from the owner. Again, always get your CARFAX history report for the details the seller may not disclose. All private sales are "as-is" unless you have a contract explicitly stating other terms.

Do your own research first on car values, sale prices, warranties, features and car history. This will save you money up front and over time. Do the due diligence and have a clearly defined list of requirements before walking into the dealership or meeting with a private seller Have stricter requirements when dealing with individuals as you have no guarantees and must look out for your interests before buying because afterwards it's too late. Being prepared is the best way to guarantee you get a good deal and a quality car.

verifyText.value: Along with your income and debt status, your personal credit profile can have a significant impact on which loans are available to you and the rates offered. A high credit rating can save you thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.
Individuals with excellent credit ratings typically have a FICO score above 740
Individuals with good credit ratings typically have a FICO score between 660 and 740
Individuals with fair credit ratings typically have a FICO score between 580 and 660
Individuals with poor credit ratings typically have a FICO score below 580

Your FICO score (an acronym for the credit scoring service, Fair Isaacs Company) is an assigned number between 300 and 850 that indicates to lenders your capacity to repay a loan. It can change regularly, as new information is sent by your creditors to one or more of the three major national credit bureaus, Experian, Trans Union, and Equifax. The higher your FICO score, the more likely you will qualify for a mortgage loan and the best interest rates.
A FICO score is comprised of 5 parts:

Your types of accounts and your payment record; any bankruptcies, legal judgments, wage garnishments, etc.; the severity and amount of late payments; the number of past-due items and when they occurred. (35%)
How much you currently owe and on what types of accounts; number of accounts with balances; the proportion of credit lines still available. (30%)
Time since accounts opened; by specific type of account; since last activity. (15%)
Number of recently opened accounts, by type and date opened; recent credit inquiries and date of inquiries; reestablishment of good credit after payment delinquencies. (10%)
The number and types of credit accounts available for your use. (10%)
By federal law, you're entitled to a free credit report once every 12 months from each of the three major credit bureaus - Experian, TransUnion, or Equifax.
